CHAPTER 31 - IMMUNOBIOLOGY: AN INTRODUCTION

Introduction

Every day our body is exposed to countless microorganisms - bacteria, viruses, fungi, protozoa - and to their toxic products, yet most of the time we remain healthy. This is because the body possesses an elaborate defence system, the IMMUNE SYSTEM, which recognises foreign invaders and destroys them. The ability of the body to resist and fight disease-causing agents is called IMMUNITY, and the branch of biology that studies it is called IMMUNOLOGY or immunobiology. This chapter introduces the cells, organs and molecules of the immune system, the two kinds of immunity (innate and acquired), the antibodies and antigens at the heart of specific defence, the use of vaccination, and the disorders that arise when the immune system is deficient, over-active or turned against the body itself.

31.1 IMMUNITY AND THE IMMUNE SYSTEM

Immunity is the capacity of the body to recognise, resist and eliminate foreign substances and pathogens while tolerating its own tissues. The immune system is not a single organ but a network of specialised cells, tissues and organs, together with soluble molecules such as antibodies, complement proteins and cytokines that circulate in blood and lymph. The white blood cells (leucocytes) are the main cells of the system; they include the phagocytes (neutrophils and macrophages), the lymphocytes (B-cells and T-cells) and other cells such as mast cells and natural killer cells. A healthy immune system must do three things well: distinguish SELF from NON-SELF, respond quickly and specifically to genuine threats, and remember past infections so that later encounters are dealt with faster.

Broadly, immunity is of two types. INNATE (non-specific, inborn) immunity is present from birth and acts against any invader in the same general way. ACQUIRED (specific, adaptive) immunity develops during a person's life after exposure to a particular pathogen or its antigen and is highly specific to it. The two systems work together, the innate system providing the first and immediate line of defence and the acquired system providing a slower but powerful and long-lasting specific response.

31.2 ANTIGENS AND ANTIBODIES

An ANTIGEN (antibody-generator) is any foreign substance, usually a large molecule such as a protein or polysaccharide, that when introduced into the body is recognised as non-self and provokes a specific immune response. Antigens are present on the surfaces of bacteria, viruses, pollen grains, transplanted tissues and toxins. The small part of an antigen that is actually recognised by an antibody or lymphocyte is called the antigenic determinant or EPITOPE. A substance too small to be antigenic by itself but which becomes antigenic when attached to a larger carrier is called a HAPTEN.

An ANTIBODY, also called an IMMUNOGLOBULIN (Ig), is a protein produced by the body (by plasma cells derived from B-lymphocytes) in response to an antigen, and it binds specifically to that antigen. Structurally an antibody is a Y-SHAPED molecule made of FOUR polypeptide chains: two identical long HEAVY chains and two identical short LIGHT chains, held together by disulphide bonds. Each chain has a VARIABLE region and a CONSTANT region. The two tips of the Y (formed by the variable regions of one heavy and one light chain) are the ANTIGEN-BINDING SITES; their amino-acid sequence differs from antibody to antibody and gives each antibody its unique specificity - it fits its antigen like a lock and key. The stem of the Y (the constant region) determines the class of the antibody and how it interacts with complement and phagocytes.

There are FIVE classes of immunoglobulins in humans:
- IgG - the most abundant antibody in blood; it provides long-term immunity, crosses the placenta to protect the foetus, and neutralises toxins and microbes.
- IgA - found in secretions such as saliva, tears, sweat, mucus and milk; it guards mucous surfaces and the newborn gut.
- IgM - the largest antibody (a pentamer of five units); it is the FIRST antibody produced in a new infection and is very effective at agglutinating microbes and activating complement.
- IgE - involved in ALLERGIC reactions and in defence against parasitic worms; it binds to mast cells and triggers the release of histamine.
- IgD - present in small amounts on the surface of B-cells, where it acts as a receptor for antigen.

When an antibody meets its antigen it may neutralise a toxin, clump (agglutinate) microbes together, coat microbes to make them easier to swallow (opsonisation), or activate the complement system - all of which help remove the invader. This antigen-antibody reaction is the basis of many diagnostic tests and of humoral immunity.

31.3 INNATE (NON-SPECIFIC) IMMUNITY

Innate immunity is the inborn, ready-made defence that acts against a wide range of invaders without being specific to any one of them, and without improving on repeated exposure. It has several lines of defence.

(a) PHYSICAL AND MECHANICAL BARRIERS. The SKIN is the largest barrier; its tough, dry, keratinised outer layer prevents most microbes from entering. Mucous membranes lining the respiratory, digestive and urinogenital tracts trap microbes in sticky MUCUS. The beating cilia of the respiratory tract sweep trapped particles out, and reflexes such as coughing and sneezing expel them.

(b) CHEMICAL BARRIERS. Various secretions kill or inhibit microbes. The acidic gastric juice (HYDROCHLORIC ACID) of the stomach destroys most swallowed bacteria. The enzyme LYSOZYME in tears, saliva and nasal secretions dissolves bacterial cell walls. Sebum and sweat make the skin slightly acidic, and the acidic environment of the vagina discourages microbial growth.

(c) CELLULAR DEFENCE (PHAGOCYTES). Microbes that get past the barriers are met by phagocytic white cells that engulf and digest them, a process called PHAGOCYTOSIS. The chief phagocytes are the NEUTROPHILS (the most numerous WBCs, first to arrive) and the MACROPHAGES (large, long-lived cells derived from monocytes that also present antigen to lymphocytes). NATURAL KILLER (NK) cells are lymphocytes of innate immunity that destroy virus-infected cells and tumour cells without prior sensitisation.

(d) INFLAMMATION. When tissue is injured or infected, the local response of INFLAMMATION sets in, marked by redness, heat, swelling and pain. Damaged cells and mast cells release chemicals such as HISTAMINE that widen blood vessels and make them leaky, so that more blood, fluid and phagocytes reach the site to wall off and clear the infection.

(e) FEVER. Chemicals called pyrogens released during infection raise the body temperature. A moderate FEVER slows the multiplication of some microbes and speeds up defensive reactions.

(f) INTERFERONS. When a cell is infected by a virus it secretes small proteins called INTERFERONS. These diffuse to neighbouring cells and make them resistant to viral multiplication, thus limiting the spread of the virus.

(g) THE COMPLEMENT SYSTEM. This is a group of about twenty plasma proteins that normally circulate in an inactive form. When activated (by microbes or by antigen-antibody complexes) they act in a cascade to punch holes in microbial membranes (lysis), to coat microbes for easier phagocytosis (opsonisation), and to promote inflammation. It thus links and reinforces both innate and acquired defence.

31.4 ACQUIRED (SPECIFIC / ADAPTIVE) IMMUNITY

Acquired immunity is the defence that develops during life against SPECIFIC antigens. It has two great hallmarks: SPECIFICITY (each response is directed at one particular antigen) and MEMORY (a second exposure to the same antigen provokes a faster, stronger response). It is carried out mainly by the LYMPHOCYTES, which are of two kinds - B-lymphocytes and T-lymphocytes - both formed in the bone marrow. Acquired immunity has two arms: humoral (antibody-mediated) immunity and cell-mediated immunity.

(a) HUMORAL (ANTIBODY-MEDIATED) IMMUNITY. This is carried out by the B-LYMPHOCYTES (B-cells), which mature in the bone marrow. When a B-cell meets the antigen that fits its surface receptor (usually with help from a helper T-cell), it is activated, multiplies and differentiates into PLASMA CELLS and memory cells. The plasma cells are antibody factories that secrete large amounts of specific antibody into the blood and lymph - the "body fluids" or humours, hence the name humoral. These circulating antibodies neutralise toxins and free microbes, so humoral immunity is especially effective against bacteria and against viruses before they enter cells.

(b) CELL-MEDIATED IMMUNITY (CMI). This is carried out by the T-LYMPHOCYTES (T-cells), which are formed in the bone marrow but mature in the THYMUS gland (hence the name T-cells). T-cells do not secrete antibodies; they act directly through cells. HELPER T-CELLS recognise antigen presented by macrophages and secrete chemical messengers (cytokines) that stimulate both B-cells and other T-cells - they are the master coordinators of the immune response. CYTOTOXIC (killer) T-CELLS directly destroy the body's own cells infected with viruses, as well as cancer cells and cells of grafted tissue. SUPPRESSOR (regulatory) T-CELLS switch off the response when the infection is over. CMI is chiefly responsible for defence against viruses, fungi and other intracellular parasites, for the rejection of grafts, and for immunity against cancer.

(c) PRIMARY AND SECONDARY IMMUNE RESPONSE. The FIRST time the body meets a particular antigen it mounts a PRIMARY RESPONSE. This is slow: after a lag of several days the amount of antibody rises gradually, reaches a modest peak (mostly IgM at first) and then falls. During this response some activated lymphocytes do not become plasma or effector cells but survive as long-lived MEMORY CELLS. If the SAME antigen enters the body again, even years later, these memory cells trigger a SECONDARY RESPONSE that is far quicker, much larger (mostly IgG) and longer-lasting than the primary response. This immunological memory is the reason we usually suffer many childhood infections only once, and it is the scientific basis of vaccination.

31.5 ACTIVE AND PASSIVE IMMUNITY; THE LYMPHOID ORGANS

Acquired immunity may be gained in two ways.

ACTIVE IMMUNITY is the immunity a person develops by his or her OWN immune system making antibodies and memory cells in response to an antigen. It may be acquired NATURALLY, by actually suffering an infection and recovering from it, or ARTIFICIALLY, by vaccination with a harmless form of the antigen. Active immunity takes time (days to weeks) to develop but is LONG-LASTING because memory cells are formed.

PASSIVE IMMUNITY is the immunity a person receives when READY-MADE antibodies are given from another source; the recipient's own system does not make them. It may be NATURAL, as when a foetus receives IgG through the placenta or a baby receives IgA in the mother's milk, or ARTIFICIAL, as when a patient is injected with antiserum (for example anti-tetanus serum or snake-bite antivenom). Passive immunity acts IMMEDIATELY, which is life-saving in an emergency, but it is SHORT-LIVED because no memory cells are formed.

THE LYMPHOID (IMMUNE) ORGANS. The cells of the immune system are produced, matured and gathered in lymphoid organs, divided into primary and secondary organs.
- BONE MARROW (primary) - the soft tissue inside bones where all blood cells, including lymphocytes, are formed from stem cells; B-cells also mature here.
- THYMUS (primary) - a gland in the chest above the heart where T-cells mature and learn to tell self from non-self; it is large in children and shrinks after puberty.
- SPLEEN (secondary) - a large abdominal organ that filters the blood, removes old and worn-out cells, and traps blood-borne microbes where lymphocytes can attack them.
- LYMPH NODES (secondary) - small bean-shaped structures along the lymph vessels that filter lymph and trap antigens, providing meeting places where lymphocytes are activated; they swell during an infection.
- Additional lymphoid tissue guards the mucous surfaces, such as the TONSILS in the throat, the Peyer's patches in the intestine and the appendix.

31.6 VACCINATION AND IMMUNISATION

VACCINATION (immunisation) is the deliberate introduction of a VACCINE - a preparation of a killed, weakened or harmless part of a pathogen - into the body so as to stimulate the immune system to produce antibodies and, above all, memory cells WITHOUT causing the disease. The vaccinated person thus develops active, artificial immunity and is protected if the real pathogen attacks later, because the secondary response deals with it swiftly. The idea goes back to Edward Jenner, who in 1796 used cowpox material to protect against smallpox, and to Louis Pasteur, who coined the word "vaccine". A vaccine works by imitating a first, harmless infection so the body forms memory without the disease.

TYPES OF VACCINES include:
- LIVE ATTENUATED vaccines, which contain living but weakened (attenuated) microbes that cannot cause serious disease - for example the BCG (tuberculosis), oral polio (Sabin), measles and MMR vaccines. They give strong, long-lasting immunity.
- KILLED (INACTIVATED) vaccines, which contain microbes killed by heat or chemicals - for example the injected (Salk) polio, cholera and whooping-cough vaccines. They are safer but often need booster doses.
- TOXOID vaccines, made from bacterial TOXINS that have been made harmless, used against diseases whose damage is caused by a toxin - for example diphtheria and tetanus toxoids.
- SUBUNIT and recombinant vaccines, which contain only a purified antigenic part of the microbe, for example the hepatitis B vaccine made by genetic engineering.

Widespread vaccination protects the individual and, when enough of a population is immunised, protects the whole community by "herd immunity", which breaks the chain of transmission. SMALLPOX has been completely eradicated from the world by vaccination, and polio has been all but eliminated.

31.7 IMMUNE DISORDERS

The immune system normally protects us, but it can malfunction in three broad ways - by over-reacting, by attacking self, or by failing.

(a) HYPERSENSITIVITY (ALLERGY). Sometimes the immune system reacts in an exaggerated way to a normally harmless substance such as pollen, dust, certain foods, or drugs. Such substances are called ALLERGENS, and the exaggerated reaction is a HYPERSENSITIVITY or ALLERGY. In a common type of allergy the allergen causes production of IgE antibodies, which attach to mast cells; on the next exposure the allergen makes these cells release HISTAMINE and other chemicals, producing sneezing, a running nose, watery eyes, itching, rashes or difficulty in breathing. Examples are hay fever, asthma and hives. A sudden, severe, whole-body allergic reaction (for example to a bee sting or penicillin) is called ANAPHYLAXIS and can be fatal. Allergies are treated with ANTIHISTAMINE drugs.

(b) AUTOIMMUNE DISORDERS. Normally the immune system tolerates the body's own molecules (self-tolerance). In an AUTOIMMUNE disease this tolerance breaks down and the immune system attacks the body's OWN cells and tissues as if they were foreign, causing damage. Examples include RHEUMATOID ARTHRITIS (the joints are attacked and become inflamed and painful), systemic lupus erythematosus (SLE), type-1 diabetes mellitus (the insulin-making cells are destroyed), and myasthenia gravis. These diseases are usually chronic and are managed by drugs that suppress the immune response.

(c) IMMUNODEFICIENCY AND AIDS. When part of the immune system is missing or weak, the condition is called IMMUNODEFICIENCY, and the person suffers repeated, severe infections. Immunodeficiency may be inherited (primary) or acquired later in life. The best-known acquired form is AIDS (Acquired Immuno-Deficiency Syndrome), caused by the HUMAN IMMUNODEFICIENCY VIRUS (HIV). HIV specifically infects and destroys the HELPER T-CELLS that coordinate the immune response. As the helper T-cell count falls, the whole immune system collapses, and the patient falls prey to "opportunistic" infections and rare cancers that a healthy person would resist easily. HIV spreads through unprotected sexual contact, infected blood or shared needles, and from an infected mother to her child. There is no complete cure, but antiretroviral drugs can control the virus and greatly prolong life.

31.8 ORGAN TRANSPLANTATION AND GRAFT REJECTION

When a diseased organ (kidney, heart, liver) is replaced by a healthy one from a donor, the transplant is called a GRAFT. Because every person's cells carry unique self-markers (the histocompatibility or HLA antigens), the recipient's immune system usually recognises the grafted tissue as foreign and attacks it - a reaction called GRAFT REJECTION, carried out mainly by cytotoxic T-cells of cell-mediated immunity. To reduce rejection, the donor and recipient are "tissue-matched" as closely as possible, and the patient is given IMMUNOSUPPRESSANT drugs that damp down the immune response - though these also make the patient more prone to infection.

31.9 MONOCLONAL ANTIBODIES

A single clone of identical plasma cells produces a single, pure kind of antibody directed against one epitope; such antibodies made in the laboratory are called MONOCLONAL ANTIBODIES. They are produced by fusing an antibody-making B-cell with a tumour cell to give an immortal "hybridoma" that multiplies indefinitely and secretes one antibody. They are used in pregnancy-test kits, in diagnosing diseases, and in treating cancers and other diseases.

SUMMARY

- Immunity is the body's ability to resist and eliminate pathogens; immunology studies it. The immune system is a network of cells (mainly leucocytes), lymphoid organs and soluble molecules.
- Immunity is of two types: innate (non-specific, inborn) and acquired (specific, adaptive), which work together.
- An antigen is a foreign molecule that provokes an immune response; an antibody (immunoglobulin) is a Y-shaped protein of two heavy and two light chains with variable (antigen-binding) and constant regions. The five classes are IgG, IgA, IgM, IgE and IgD.
- Innate immunity includes physical barriers (skin, mucus, cilia), chemical barriers (stomach acid, lysozyme), phagocytes (neutrophils, macrophages), natural killer cells, inflammation, fever, interferons and the complement system.
- Acquired immunity is specific and has memory. Humoral immunity is by B-lymphocytes, which become antibody-secreting plasma cells; cell-mediated immunity is by T-lymphocytes (helper, cytotoxic, suppressor), which mature in the thymus.
- A first meeting with an antigen gives a slow primary response and leaves memory cells; a second meeting gives a rapid, strong secondary response - the basis of vaccination.
- Active immunity (own antibodies, slow but lasting) and passive immunity (ready-made antibodies, immediate but short-lived) each occur in natural and artificial forms.
- Lymphoid organs: bone marrow and thymus (primary), spleen, lymph nodes, tonsils (secondary).
- Vaccination gives active artificial immunity using live attenuated, killed, toxoid or subunit vaccines; it eradicated smallpox.
- Immune disorders: allergy (IgE, histamine, anaphylaxis), autoimmune diseases (rheumatoid arthritis, SLE, type-1 diabetes), and immunodeficiency including AIDS, in which HIV destroys helper T-cells.
- Graft rejection is a cell-mediated attack on transplanted tissue, reduced by tissue-matching and immunosuppressant drugs. Monoclonal antibodies are pure single antibodies made by hybridomas.

worksheet.title: Worksheet - Immunobiology: An Introduction (NIOS Senior Secondary Biology)
worksheet.instructions: Attempt all questions. Short-answer questions carry 2-3 marks and long-answer questions carry 5 marks. Write biological terms clearly and, where asked, give examples.

questions.question: Define immunity and name the two broad types of immunity.
questions.answer: Immunity is the ability of the body to recognise, resist and eliminate foreign substances and disease-causing organisms while tolerating its own tissues. The two broad types are (1) innate (non-specific, inborn) immunity, which is present from birth and acts against any invader in the same general way, and (2) acquired (specific, adaptive) immunity, which develops during life against particular antigens and shows specificity and memory.
questions.explanation: Definition plus the innate/acquired classification.

questions.question: Describe the structure of an antibody with reference to its chains and regions.
questions.answer: An antibody (immunoglobulin) is a Y-shaped protein made of four polypeptide chains: two identical long heavy chains and two identical short light chains, held together by disulphide bonds. Each chain has a variable region and a constant region. The two tips of the Y are formed by the variable regions and are the antigen-binding sites, which give the antibody its specificity (lock-and-key fit for its antigen). The stem of the Y is the constant region, which determines the antibody class and its interaction with complement and phagocytes.
questions.explanation: Y-shape, 2 heavy + 2 light chains, variable/constant regions, binding sites.

questions.question: List any three physical or chemical barriers of innate immunity and state how each protects the body.
questions.answer: (1) Skin - its tough, dry, keratinised outer layer forms a physical barrier that prevents most microbes from entering the body. (2) Mucus lining the respiratory and digestive tracts traps microbes, and beating cilia sweep them out. (3) Stomach acid (hydrochloric acid) - the acidic gastric juice kills most bacteria swallowed with food. (Lysozyme in tears and saliva, which dissolves bacterial cell walls, is another acceptable chemical barrier.)
questions.explanation: Any three barriers with their protective action.

questions.question: Distinguish between humoral immunity and cell-mediated immunity.
questions.answer: Humoral (antibody-mediated) immunity is carried out by B-lymphocytes, which on activation become plasma cells that secrete specific antibodies into the blood and lymph; it acts against free microbes and toxins in body fluids. Cell-mediated immunity is carried out by T-lymphocytes (which mature in the thymus); these do not secrete antibodies but act directly - helper T-cells coordinate the response, cytotoxic T-cells kill infected or cancerous cells, and it defends against intracellular pathogens, grafts and cancer.
questions.explanation: B-cells/antibodies vs T-cells/direct action.

questions.question: Why is the secondary immune response faster and stronger than the primary response?
questions.answer: During the primary response (the first exposure to an antigen) some activated lymphocytes survive as long-lived memory cells instead of becoming effector cells. When the same antigen enters again, these memory cells recognise it at once and multiply rapidly, so the secondary response has almost no lag, produces much more antibody (mostly IgG) and lasts longer. This immunological memory is why we suffer many infections only once and is the basis of vaccination.
questions.explanation: Memory cells from the primary response drive the faster secondary response.

questions.question: Differentiate between active and passive immunity, giving one example of each.
questions.answer: Active immunity is produced by a person's own immune system making antibodies and memory cells in response to an antigen; it develops slowly but is long-lasting. Example: immunity after recovering from measles, or after vaccination. Passive immunity is received as ready-made antibodies from another source, so the recipient's own system does not make them; it acts immediately but is short-lived because no memory cells form. Example: antibodies passed to a foetus through the placenta, or an injection of anti-tetanus serum.
questions.explanation: Own vs borrowed antibodies; slow-lasting vs immediate-short.

questions.question: Name the primary and secondary lymphoid organs and state one function of the thymus.
questions.answer: The primary lymphoid organs are the bone marrow and the thymus. The secondary lymphoid organs are the spleen, the lymph nodes and the tonsils (with other mucosal lymphoid tissue). Function of the thymus: it is the gland in the chest where T-lymphocytes mature and learn to distinguish self from non-self; it is large in children and shrinks after puberty.
questions.explanation: Primary (marrow, thymus), secondary (spleen, nodes, tonsils); thymus matures T-cells.

questions.question: Explain the principle of vaccination and describe the main types of vaccines with an example of each.
questions.answer:
Principle: Vaccination introduces a vaccine - a killed, weakened or harmless part of a pathogen - into the body. This imitates a first, harmless infection and stimulates the immune system to produce antibodies and, above all, memory cells, without causing the disease. The person thus gains active artificial immunity; if the real pathogen attacks later, the rapid secondary response deals with it before illness develops.

Main types of vaccines:
(1) Live attenuated vaccines contain living but weakened microbes that cannot cause serious disease and give strong, long-lasting immunity - e.g. BCG (tuberculosis), oral polio (Sabin), measles/MMR.
(2) Killed (inactivated) vaccines contain microbes killed by heat or chemicals; they are safer but often need booster doses - e.g. injected (Salk) polio, cholera, whooping cough.
(3) Toxoid vaccines are made from bacterial toxins rendered harmless, used where damage is caused by a toxin - e.g. diphtheria and tetanus toxoids.
(4) Subunit/recombinant vaccines contain only a purified antigenic part of the microbe - e.g. hepatitis B vaccine made by genetic engineering.

When enough people are vaccinated, herd immunity protects the whole community. Vaccination has eradicated smallpox from the world.
questions.explanation: Principle (memory without disease) plus four vaccine types with examples.

questions.question: What is an allergy? Name the antibody and the chemical involved in a typical allergic reaction.
questions.answer: An allergy (hypersensitivity) is an exaggerated, harmful immune reaction to a normally harmless substance called an allergen (for example pollen, dust or certain foods). In a common type of allergy the allergen causes the production of IgE antibodies, which attach to mast cells; on the next exposure the allergen makes these cells release histamine and other chemicals, producing sneezing, running nose, watery eyes, itching or difficulty in breathing. A sudden severe whole-body reaction is called anaphylaxis. So the antibody is IgE and the chemical is histamine.
questions.explanation: Definition, allergen, IgE and histamine.

questions.question: How does HIV cause AIDS? Explain why an AIDS patient becomes prone to many other infections, and briefly state what graft rejection is.
questions.answer:
AIDS (Acquired Immuno-Deficiency Syndrome) is caused by the Human Immunodeficiency Virus (HIV). HIV specifically infects and destroys the helper T-cells, which are the master coordinators of the immune response - they stimulate both B-cells and other T-cells through cytokines. As HIV multiplies, the helper T-cell count steadily falls. Without helper T-cells the whole immune response - both humoral and cell-mediated - cannot be organised properly, so the immune system collapses. The patient therefore falls prey to 'opportunistic' infections and rare cancers that a healthy immune system would easily resist; it is usually these secondary infections, rather than HIV itself, that prove fatal. HIV spreads through unprotected sexual contact, infected blood or shared needles and from an infected mother to her child; antiretroviral drugs can control it but there is no complete cure.

Graft rejection: when a healthy organ (graft) is transplanted from a donor, the recipient's immune system recognises the foreign HLA (self-marker) antigens on the grafted tissue and attacks it, mainly through cytotoxic T-cells of cell-mediated immunity. This destruction of the transplant is called graft rejection; it is reduced by tissue-matching donor and recipient and by giving immunosuppressant drugs.
questions.explanation: HIV destroys helper T-cells -> immune collapse -> opportunistic infections; graft rejection by cytotoxic T-cells.

questions.question: What is meant by the immune system?
questions.answer: The immune system is the body's network of specialised cells (mainly the white blood cells), tissues and lymphoid organs, together with soluble molecules such as antibodies, complement proteins and cytokines, that together recognise foreign invaders and destroy them while tolerating the body's own tissues.
questions.explanation: Cells + organs + soluble molecules that defend the body.

questions.question: State two differences between innate and acquired immunity.
questions.answer: (1) Innate immunity is inborn and present from birth, whereas acquired immunity develops during life after exposure to an antigen. (2) Innate immunity is non-specific (acts the same way against all invaders and does not improve on repeat exposure), whereas acquired immunity is specific to a particular antigen and shows memory, giving a stronger response on re-exposure.
questions.explanation: Inborn/non-specific vs developed/specific-with-memory.

questions.question: What is an antigen? Give one example.
questions.answer: An antigen is any foreign substance, usually a large molecule such as a protein or polysaccharide, that when introduced into the body is recognised as non-self and provokes a specific immune response. Examples include the surface proteins of bacteria and viruses, pollen grains, and toxins.
questions.explanation: Definition plus example (bacterial surface protein, pollen, toxin).

questions.question: Name the five classes of immunoglobulins and give one function of each.
questions.answer: (1) IgG - the most abundant antibody in blood; gives long-term immunity and crosses the placenta. (2) IgA - found in secretions (saliva, tears, milk, mucus); guards mucous surfaces. (3) IgM - the largest antibody; the first produced in a new infection and good at agglutinating microbes. (4) IgE - involved in allergic reactions and defence against parasitic worms. (5) IgD - present on the surface of B-cells as an antigen receptor.
questions.explanation: IgG, IgA, IgM, IgE, IgD each with a function.

questions.question: Distinguish between the variable and constant regions of an antibody.
questions.answer: The variable region lies at the two tips of the Y and differs from antibody to antibody; its amino-acid sequence forms the antigen-binding sites and gives each antibody its specificity. The constant region forms the stem (and lower parts) of the Y; it is the same within an antibody class and determines the class of the antibody and how it interacts with complement and phagocytes.
questions.explanation: Variable = binding/specificity; constant = class/effector functions.

questions.question: In what ways can an antibody help to destroy or remove an invading microbe?
questions.answer: When an antibody binds its antigen it may (1) neutralise a toxin by blocking its active part; (2) agglutinate (clump) microbes together so they are easier to remove; (3) precipitate soluble antigens out of solution; (4) coat microbes (opsonisation) so that phagocytes swallow them more readily; and (5) activate the complement system, which lyses microbes and promotes inflammation. All of these help destroy or clear the invader.
questions.explanation: Neutralisation, agglutination, precipitation, opsonisation, complement activation.

questions.question: What are phagocytes? Name two types.
questions.answer: Phagocytes are white blood cells that engulf and digest microbes and cell debris by a process called phagocytosis. Two important types are neutrophils (the most numerous WBCs, first to arrive at an infection) and macrophages (large, long-lived cells derived from monocytes that also present antigen to lymphocytes).
questions.explanation: Phagocytes engulf microbes; neutrophils and macrophages.

questions.question: Describe inflammation and state its usefulness.
questions.answer: Inflammation is the local response of a tissue to injury or infection, marked by four signs: redness, heat, swelling and pain. Damaged cells and mast cells release chemicals such as histamine that widen blood vessels and make them leaky. As a result more blood, fluid and phagocytes reach the site, where they wall off and clear the infection and begin repair. Inflammation is therefore a useful defensive reaction that concentrates the body's defences at the point of damage.
questions.explanation: Signs (redness, heat, swelling, pain), histamine, more phagocytes to clear infection.

questions.question: What are interferons and what do they do?
questions.answer: Interferons are small proteins secreted by a body cell when it is infected by a virus. They diffuse to neighbouring, still-healthy cells and make them resistant to viral multiplication, thereby limiting the spread of the virus. They are an important part of innate (non-specific) antiviral defence.
questions.explanation: Proteins from virus-infected cells that protect neighbours.

questions.question: How does the complement system reinforce immunity?
questions.answer: The complement system is a group of about twenty plasma proteins that normally circulate in an inactive form. When activated (by microbes or by antigen-antibody complexes) they act in a cascade. They (1) punch holes in microbial membranes, causing lysis; (2) coat microbes (opsonisation) so phagocytes engulf them more easily; and (3) promote inflammation, drawing in more defensive cells. Because it can be triggered both by microbes directly and by antibodies, complement links and reinforces both innate and acquired immunity.
questions.explanation: Lysis, opsonisation, inflammation; links innate and acquired defence.

questions.question: What is humoral immunity?
questions.answer: Humoral (antibody-mediated) immunity is the arm of acquired immunity carried out by B-lymphocytes. When a B-cell is activated by its antigen it multiplies and differentiates into plasma cells, which secrete large amounts of specific antibody into the blood and lymph (the body 'humours'). These circulating antibodies neutralise toxins and free microbes, so humoral immunity is especially effective against bacteria and against viruses before they enter cells.
questions.explanation: B-cells -> plasma cells -> antibodies against free microbes.

questions.question: Describe the different kinds of T-cells and their roles.
questions.answer: T-lymphocytes mature in the thymus and carry out cell-mediated immunity. Helper T-cells recognise antigen presented by macrophages and secrete cytokines that stimulate both B-cells and other T-cells - they coordinate the whole response. Cytotoxic (killer) T-cells directly recognise and destroy the body's own cells that are infected with viruses, as well as cancer cells and cells of grafted tissue. Suppressor (regulatory) T-cells switch off the immune response once the infection is over.
questions.explanation: Helper (coordinate), cytotoxic (kill), suppressor (switch off).

questions.question: Against what kinds of threats is cell-mediated immunity chiefly effective?
questions.answer: Cell-mediated immunity is chiefly effective against intracellular threats and abnormal cells: viruses and other intracellular parasites (such as some fungi and protozoa), the body's own virus-infected cells, cancer cells, and the cells of transplanted (grafted) tissue, which it attacks in graft rejection.
questions.explanation: Intracellular pathogens, infected cells, cancer, grafts.

questions.question: Compare the primary and secondary immune responses.
questions.answer: The primary response occurs on the first exposure to an antigen. It is slow: after a lag of several days the antibody level rises gradually to a modest peak (mostly IgM) and then falls; some cells survive as memory cells. The secondary response occurs when the same antigen is met again. Because memory cells are already present, it has almost no lag, rises quickly to a much higher peak (mostly IgG) and lasts longer. Thus the secondary response is faster, larger and more durable than the primary.
questions.explanation: Primary: slow, small, IgM; secondary: fast, large, IgG (from memory cells).

questions.question: Explain how immunological memory forms the basis of vaccination.
questions.answer: During a first exposure to an antigen the immune system makes some long-lived memory cells in addition to effector cells. A vaccine deliberately supplies a harmless form of a pathogen's antigen, so the body forms memory cells without suffering the disease. If the real pathogen later enters the body, these memory cells trigger a rapid, powerful secondary response that destroys it before illness develops. Thus vaccination works precisely because of immunological memory.
questions.explanation: Vaccine builds memory cells -> rapid secondary response on real infection.

questions.question: Give two examples of naturally acquired passive immunity.
questions.answer: (1) The transfer of IgG antibodies from a mother to her foetus across the placenta before birth. (2) The transfer of IgA antibodies from a mother to her baby through breast milk. In both cases the baby receives ready-made antibodies rather than making its own, so the immunity is passive and natural.
questions.explanation: Placental IgG and IgA in breast milk.

questions.question: Compare active and passive immunity in terms of source, speed and duration.
questions.answer: Active immunity is made by a person's own immune system (after infection or vaccination); it develops slowly, over days to weeks, but is long-lasting because memory cells are formed. Passive immunity is received as ready-made antibodies from another source (placenta, milk or an antiserum injection); it acts immediately, which is valuable in emergencies, but is short-lived because the borrowed antibodies are gradually destroyed and no memory cells form.
questions.explanation: Source (own vs borrowed), speed (slow vs immediate), duration (long vs short).

questions.question: Name the lymphoid organs and classify them as primary or secondary.
questions.answer: Primary lymphoid organs (where lymphocytes are produced and mature): the bone marrow (all blood cells form here; B-cells also mature here) and the thymus (where T-cells mature). Secondary lymphoid organs (where lymphocytes meet antigen and are activated): the spleen (filters blood), the lymph nodes (filter lymph) and the tonsils, with other mucosal lymphoid tissue such as Peyer's patches and the appendix.
questions.explanation: Primary: bone marrow, thymus. Secondary: spleen, lymph nodes, tonsils.

questions.question: What is a vaccine? Explain how vaccination protects a person from a disease.
questions.answer: A vaccine is a preparation of a killed, weakened (attenuated) or harmless part of a pathogen. When it is introduced into the body, it stimulates the immune system to produce antibodies and, above all, memory cells, without causing the disease. The person thus gains active artificial immunity. If the real pathogen attacks later, the memory cells mount a rapid, strong secondary response that destroys it before the disease can develop, so the person is protected.
questions.explanation: Vaccine builds memory without disease -> fast secondary response on real infection.

questions.question: Name the four main types of vaccines.
questions.answer: The four main types are (1) live attenuated vaccines (living but weakened microbes, e.g. BCG, oral polio), (2) killed/inactivated vaccines (microbes killed by heat or chemicals, e.g. Salk polio, cholera), (3) toxoid vaccines (inactivated bacterial toxins, e.g. tetanus, diphtheria), and (4) subunit/recombinant vaccines (only a purified antigenic part, e.g. hepatitis B).
questions.explanation: Attenuated, killed, toxoid, subunit/recombinant.

questions.question: What is an autoimmune disease? Give one example.
questions.answer: An autoimmune disease is one in which the immune system's tolerance of the body's own molecules breaks down, so it attacks the body's own cells and tissues as if they were foreign, causing damage. An example is rheumatoid arthritis, in which the joints are attacked and become inflamed and painful (other examples are SLE and type-1 diabetes).
questions.explanation: Immune attack on self; example rheumatoid arthritis.

questions.question: What are monoclonal antibodies and where are they used?
questions.answer: Monoclonal antibodies are pure, identical antibodies directed against a single epitope, produced in the laboratory by fusing an antibody-making B-cell with a tumour cell to form an immortal 'hybridoma' that multiplies indefinitely and secretes one kind of antibody. They are used in pregnancy-test kits, in diagnosing diseases, in identifying cells, and increasingly in treating cancers and other diseases.
questions.explanation: Single pure antibody from a hybridoma; used in diagnosis and therapy.

questions.question: Describe the structure of an antibody molecule and list the five classes of immunoglobulins with their functions.
questions.answer:
Structure: An antibody (immunoglobulin) is a Y-shaped protein made of four polypeptide chains held together by disulphide bonds - two identical long heavy chains and two identical short light chains. Each chain has a variable region and a constant region. The two tips of the Y are formed by the variable regions of a heavy and a light chain and are the antigen-binding sites; their amino-acid sequence differs from antibody to antibody and gives each antibody its unique specificity, so that it fits its antigen like a lock and key. The stem of the Y is the constant region, which determines the class of the antibody and how it interacts with complement and phagocytes.

Five classes:
(1) IgG - the most abundant antibody in blood; gives long-term immunity, crosses the placenta to protect the foetus, and neutralises toxins and microbes.
(2) IgA - found in secretions such as saliva, tears, sweat, mucus and milk; guards mucous surfaces and the newborn gut.
(3) IgM - the largest antibody (a pentamer of five units); the first antibody produced in a new infection, very good at agglutinating microbes and activating complement.
(4) IgE - involved in allergic reactions and defence against parasitic worms; binds to mast cells and triggers histamine release.
(5) IgD - present in small amounts on the surface of B-cells, where it acts as an antigen receptor.
questions.explanation: Y-shape (2 heavy + 2 light, variable/constant, binding sites) plus the five Ig classes with roles.

questions.question: Describe the various components of innate (non-specific) immunity.
questions.answer:
Innate immunity is the inborn, ready-made defence that acts against many invaders in the same general way. Its components are:
(a) Physical/mechanical barriers - the skin (tough, dry, keratinised) keeps most microbes out; mucus in the respiratory and digestive tracts traps microbes, and beating cilia and reflexes such as coughing and sneezing expel them.
(b) Chemical barriers - hydrochloric acid in the stomach destroys most swallowed bacteria; the enzyme lysozyme in tears and saliva dissolves bacterial cell walls; acidic sebum, sweat and vaginal secretions discourage microbes.
(c) Cellular defence - phagocytes engulf and digest microbes by phagocytosis; the chief phagocytes are neutrophils (most numerous, first to arrive) and macrophages (large, long-lived, also present antigen). Natural killer (NK) cells destroy virus-infected and tumour cells without prior sensitisation.
(d) Inflammation - injured tissue shows redness, heat, swelling and pain; histamine widens leaky vessels so more phagocytes reach and clear the site.
(e) Fever - pyrogens raise body temperature, slowing microbial multiplication and speeding defence.
(f) Interferons - proteins from virus-infected cells that make neighbouring cells resist the virus.
(g) Complement system - about twenty plasma proteins that, when activated, lyse microbes, opsonise them for phagocytosis and promote inflammation.
questions.explanation: Barriers (physical, chemical), phagocytes, NK cells, inflammation, fever, interferons, complement.

questions.question: Distinguish between humoral and cell-mediated immunity, describing the cells involved in each.
questions.answer:
Both are arms of acquired (specific) immunity, but they use different cells and act in different ways.

Humoral (antibody-mediated) immunity is carried out by B-lymphocytes, which mature in the bone marrow. When a B-cell meets the antigen that fits its surface receptor (usually with help from a helper T-cell), it is activated and multiplies, differentiating into plasma cells and memory cells. Plasma cells are antibody factories that secrete large amounts of specific antibody into the blood and lymph (the body 'humours'). These circulating antibodies neutralise toxins and free microbes, so humoral immunity is especially effective against bacteria and against viruses before they enter cells.

Cell-mediated immunity (CMI) is carried out by T-lymphocytes, which form in the bone marrow but mature in the thymus. T-cells do not secrete antibodies; they act directly through cells. Helper T-cells recognise antigen presented by macrophages and secrete cytokines that stimulate B-cells and other T-cells - they coordinate the response. Cytotoxic (killer) T-cells directly destroy virus-infected cells, cancer cells and cells of grafted tissue. Suppressor (regulatory) T-cells switch off the response when infection is over. CMI is chiefly responsible for defence against intracellular pathogens, for graft rejection and for immunity against cancer.
questions.explanation: Humoral = B-cells/plasma cells/antibodies vs CMI = T-cells (helper, cytotoxic, suppressor) acting directly.

questions.question: Explain the primary and secondary immune responses and the role of memory cells, and relate them to vaccination.
questions.answer:
When the body meets a particular antigen for the first time it mounts a primary response. This is slow: after a lag of several days, during which the specific lymphocytes are selected and multiply, the antibody level rises gradually to a modest peak (mostly IgM at first) and then declines. Crucially, some of the activated lymphocytes do not become short-lived effector (plasma or killer) cells but survive for years as memory cells.

If the same antigen enters the body again, these memory cells recognise it at once and divide rapidly, producing a secondary response. This response has almost no lag, rises to a much higher antibody level (mostly IgG) and lasts far longer than the primary response. This property is called immunological memory, and it is why we usually suffer many childhood infections only once.

Vaccination exploits this memory. A vaccine supplies a harmless form of a pathogen's antigen so that the body makes memory cells without suffering the disease. If the real pathogen later invades, the memory cells trigger a rapid, powerful secondary response that destroys it before illness can develop. Thus the primary/secondary response and memory cells are the biological basis of vaccination.
questions.explanation: Primary (slow, IgM, makes memory) vs secondary (fast, IgG); memory cells underlie vaccination.

questions.question: Distinguish between active and passive immunity (natural and artificial) and describe the lymphoid organs.
questions.answer:
Active immunity is produced by a person's own immune system making antibodies and memory cells in response to an antigen. It may be natural (acquired by suffering and recovering from an infection) or artificial (acquired by vaccination). It develops slowly but is long-lasting because memory cells form.

Passive immunity is received as ready-made antibodies from another source, so the recipient's own system does not make them. It may be natural (a foetus receiving IgG through the placenta, or a baby receiving IgA in breast milk) or artificial (a patient injected with antiserum, e.g. anti-tetanus serum or antivenom). It acts immediately, which is life-saving in emergencies, but is short-lived because no memory cells form and the borrowed antibodies are gradually destroyed.

Lymphoid organs produce, mature and gather immune cells. Primary organs: the bone marrow (where all blood cells form and B-cells mature) and the thymus (where T-cells mature and learn self from non-self; it is large in children and shrinks after puberty). Secondary organs: the spleen (filters blood, removes old cells and traps blood-borne microbes), the lymph nodes (bean-shaped filters of lymph that trap antigens and swell during infection), and the tonsils and other mucosal lymphoid tissue (Peyer's patches, appendix).
questions.explanation: Active (own, natural/artificial, lasting) vs passive (borrowed, natural/artificial, short); primary and secondary lymphoid organs described.

questions.question: What is vaccination? Explain its principle and describe the main types of vaccines, giving examples.
questions.answer:
Vaccination (immunisation) is the deliberate introduction of a vaccine - a preparation of a killed, weakened or harmless part of a pathogen - into the body to stimulate protective immunity.

Principle: The vaccine imitates a first, harmless infection. It stimulates the immune system to produce antibodies and, above all, memory cells, without causing the disease. The person thus develops active artificial immunity. If the real pathogen later invades, the memory cells mount a rapid, powerful secondary response that destroys it before illness develops. The idea goes back to Edward Jenner (cowpox against smallpox, 1796) and Louis Pasteur, who coined the word 'vaccine'.

Types of vaccines:
(1) Live attenuated - living but weakened microbes that give strong, long-lasting immunity, e.g. BCG (tuberculosis), oral polio (Sabin), measles/MMR.
(2) Killed (inactivated) - microbes killed by heat or chemicals; safer but often need boosters, e.g. Salk polio, cholera, whooping cough.
(3) Toxoid - bacterial toxins made harmless, used where damage is by a toxin, e.g. diphtheria and tetanus toxoids.
(4) Subunit/recombinant - only a purified antigenic part, e.g. hepatitis B vaccine made by genetic engineering.

When enough people are immunised, herd immunity protects even the unvaccinated by breaking transmission. Vaccination has eradicated smallpox and nearly eliminated polio.
questions.explanation: Definition, principle (memory without disease), Jenner/Pasteur, four vaccine types with examples, herd immunity.

questions.question: Describe the three main kinds of immune malfunction - hypersensitivity, autoimmunity and immunodeficiency - with examples.
questions.answer:
The immune system, though protective, can malfunction in three broad ways.

(1) Hypersensitivity (allergy): here the immune system over-reacts to a normally harmless substance called an allergen (pollen, dust, some foods or drugs). Commonly the allergen causes IgE production; the IgE attaches to mast cells, and on the next exposure the allergen makes these cells release histamine and other chemicals, producing sneezing, running nose, watery eyes, itching, rashes or breathing difficulty (hay fever, asthma, hives). A sudden, severe, whole-body reaction, e.g. to a bee sting or penicillin, is anaphylaxis, which can be fatal. Allergies are treated with antihistamine drugs.

(2) Autoimmunity: normally the body tolerates its own molecules, but in autoimmune disease this self-tolerance breaks down and the immune system attacks the body's own cells and tissues. Examples are rheumatoid arthritis (joints attacked), systemic lupus erythematosus (SLE), type-1 diabetes (insulin-making cells destroyed) and myasthenia gravis. These chronic diseases are managed with immunosuppressive drugs.

(3) Immunodeficiency: here part of the immune system is missing or weak, so infections are repeated and severe. It may be inherited (primary) or acquired. The best-known acquired form is AIDS, caused by HIV, which specifically destroys the helper T-cells that coordinate immunity; as their number falls the whole system collapses and the patient falls prey to opportunistic infections and rare cancers. HIV spreads through unprotected sex, infected blood or shared needles and from mother to child; antiretroviral drugs control but do not cure it.
questions.explanation: Hypersensitivity (IgE, histamine, anaphylaxis), autoimmunity (rheumatoid arthritis, SLE), immunodeficiency/AIDS (HIV kills helper T-cells).

questions.question: What is immunity? Explain the two broad types of immunity and how they work together to defend the body.
questions.answer:
Immunity is the capacity of the body to recognise, resist and eliminate foreign substances and disease-causing organisms while tolerating its own tissues. It is provided by the immune system - a network of white blood cells, lymphoid organs and soluble molecules such as antibodies, complement and cytokines.

Immunity is of two broad types. Innate (non-specific, inborn) immunity is present from birth and acts against any invader in the same general way, without improving on repeated exposure. It includes physical and chemical barriers (skin, mucus, stomach acid, lysozyme), phagocytes and natural killer cells, inflammation, fever, interferons and the complement system. Because it is always ready, it forms the first and immediate line of defence.

Acquired (specific, adaptive) immunity develops during a person's life after exposure to a particular antigen. Its two hallmarks are specificity (each response is aimed at one antigen) and memory (a second exposure gives a faster, stronger response). It is carried out by B- and T-lymphocytes through humoral and cell-mediated responses.

The two systems work together: the innate system contains an infection at once and also 'presents' antigens (e.g. by macrophages) that switch on the slower but powerful and long-lasting specific acquired response. Together they give the body a layered, effective defence.
questions.explanation: Definition; innate (immediate, non-specific) and acquired (specific, memory); they cooperate as layered defence.

questions.question: A student is shown a diagram of a Y-shaped antibody molecule. The two tips of the Y are labelled X and the stem is labelled Z. The antibody is said to fit its antigen like a lock and key. (a) How many heavy and light chains make up the molecule? (b) What is the correct name for the sites at X? (c) Which region, X or Z, gives the antibody its specificity? (d) What does the region at Z determine?
questions.answer: (a) The molecule is made of four chains: two heavy chains and two light chains. (b) The sites at X (the two tips of the Y) are the antigen-binding sites, formed by the variable regions. (c) The region at X (the variable region) gives the antibody its specificity, so it fits its antigen like a lock and key. (d) The region at Z (the constant region, the stem) determines the class of the antibody and how it interacts with complement and phagocytes.
questions.explanation: Tests antibody structure: chains, binding sites (variable), constant region function.

questions.question: A person cuts a finger with a dirty knife. Within hours the area around the cut becomes red, warm, swollen and painful, and pus (dead white cells and microbes) forms. (a) What is this local defensive response called? (b) Name the chemical that widens the blood vessels here. (c) Which white cells engulf the microbes at the wound? (d) State whether this defence is innate or acquired.
questions.answer: (a) The response is inflammation. (b) The chemical is histamine, released by damaged cells and mast cells, which widens blood vessels and makes them leaky. (c) Phagocytes - chiefly neutrophils (first to arrive) and macrophages - engulf and digest the microbes by phagocytosis; the dead phagocytes and microbes form pus. (d) This defence is part of innate (non-specific) immunity.
questions.explanation: Applies inflammation, histamine, phagocytes and the innate classification to a wound.

questions.question: A child is given a first dose of a vaccine. Blood tests show that antibody appears only after about a week, rises slowly to a low level, then falls. Weeks later a second (booster) dose is given, and this time antibody appears within a day or two and rises to a much higher level. (a) Name the response to the first dose. (b) Name the response to the booster dose. (c) Which cells are responsible for the faster second response? (d) Which antibody class dominates the second response?
questions.answer: (a) The response to the first dose is the primary immune response, which is slow with a lag and a low peak. (b) The response to the booster dose is the secondary immune response, which is rapid and much stronger. (c) The faster second response is due to memory cells formed during the primary response, which recognise the antigen at once and multiply rapidly. (d) The secondary response is dominated by IgG antibody (the primary response is dominated early by IgM).
questions.explanation: Analyses primary vs secondary responses, memory cells and antibody classes.

questions.question: A newborn baby is protected against some diseases in its first months by antibodies received from its mother across the placenta and in breast milk. Later, the same child is given the DPT vaccine so that it makes its own protection. (a) Name the type of immunity the baby gets from its mother. (b) Is it natural or artificial? (c) Name the type of immunity produced by the DPT vaccine. (d) Which of the two lasts longer, and why?
questions.answer: (a) The immunity received from the mother is passive immunity (the baby gets ready-made antibodies). (b) It is natural passive immunity (through the placenta and breast milk). (c) The DPT vaccine produces active artificial immunity, because the baby's own immune system makes antibodies and memory cells. (d) The active immunity from the vaccine lasts longer, because memory cells are formed; the passive immunity from the mother is short-lived, as no memory cells form and the borrowed antibodies are gradually broken down.
questions.explanation: Applies active/passive and natural/artificial immunity and their durations.

questions.question: A health worker administers several vaccines: BCG (a living weakened microbe), the tetanus vaccine (an inactivated toxin), the Salk polio vaccine (killed virus) and the hepatitis B vaccine (a purified antigen made by genetic engineering). (a) Classify each vaccine by type. (b) Which type generally gives the strongest, longest-lasting immunity? (c) What kind of immunity does vaccination produce? (d) Name the disease that vaccination has eradicated worldwide.
questions.answer: (a) BCG is a live attenuated vaccine; the tetanus vaccine is a toxoid vaccine; the Salk polio vaccine is a killed (inactivated) vaccine; the hepatitis B vaccine is a subunit/recombinant vaccine. (b) Live attenuated vaccines generally give the strongest, longest-lasting immunity. (c) Vaccination produces active artificial immunity. (d) Vaccination has eradicated smallpox worldwide.
questions.explanation: Applies the classification of vaccine types and the outcomes of vaccination.

questions.question: A person infected with HIV appears healthy for years, but blood tests show a slow fall in the number of helper T-cells. Eventually the count drops very low and the person begins to suffer repeated infections by microbes that rarely trouble healthy people, and develops rare cancers. (a) Name the syndrome that develops. (b) Which specific immune cells does HIV destroy? (c) Why do these 'opportunistic' infections take hold? (d) State one way HIV spreads.
questions.answer: (a) The syndrome that develops is AIDS (Acquired Immuno-Deficiency Syndrome). (b) HIV specifically infects and destroys the helper T-cells. (c) Helper T-cells coordinate both humoral and cell-mediated responses; as they are destroyed the whole immune system can no longer be organised and collapses, so microbes that a healthy immune system would easily resist ('opportunistic' infections) and rare cancers are able to take hold. (d) HIV spreads through unprotected sexual contact (also through infected blood or shared needles, or from an infected mother to her child).
questions.explanation: Analyses how HIV destroys helper T-cells and causes opportunistic infection; transmission route.

questions.question: A patient with kidney failure receives a kidney transplant from an unrelated donor. Despite careful surgery, the patient's body begins to attack and damage the new kidney, and the doctors prescribe drugs that damp down the immune system. (a) What is the transplanted organ called? (b) What is the reaction of the body against it called? (c) Which cells mainly carry out this reaction? (d) Name the class of drugs used to reduce it, and state one drawback.
questions.answer: (a) The transplanted organ is called a graft. (b) The reaction of the body against it is called graft rejection. (c) It is carried out mainly by the cytotoxic T-cells of cell-mediated immunity, which recognise the foreign HLA self-markers on the grafted tissue. (d) The drugs used are immunosuppressant (immunosuppressive) drugs; a drawback is that by damping down the whole immune system they make the patient more prone to infections.
questions.explanation: Analyses graft rejection, the cells involved and immunosuppressant drugs with their drawback.

questions.question: Two students argue about defence against disease. One says the body has an inborn defence that works at once against any germ; the other says the body also builds a special defence against each particular germ that it remembers. Both are partly right. (a) Name the type of immunity the first student describes. (b) Name the type described by the second student. (c) Give the two hallmarks of the second type. (d) State one way the two types cooperate.
questions.answer: (a) The first student describes innate (non-specific, inborn) immunity, which is present from birth and acts against any invader at once. (b) The second student describes acquired (specific, adaptive) immunity, which develops against particular antigens. (c) The two hallmarks of acquired immunity are specificity (each response is aimed at one antigen) and memory (a second exposure gives a faster, stronger response). (d) They cooperate, for example, when macrophages of the innate system engulf a microbe and present its antigen to lymphocytes, switching on the specific acquired response (any similar valid example is acceptable).
questions.explanation: Distinguishes innate and acquired immunity and their cooperation.

questions.question: During a viral cold, a person develops a mild fever, and cells lining the nose that are infected release small proteins that protect nearby cells from the virus. Meanwhile mucus and cilia in the airway trap and sweep out microbes. (a) Name the small protective proteins released by the infected cells. (b) How do these proteins help? (c) How does a mild fever help defence? (d) Are mucus and cilia physical or chemical barriers?
questions.answer: (a) The small proteins are interferons. (b) Interferons diffuse to neighbouring, still-healthy cells and make them resistant to viral multiplication, thus limiting the spread of the virus. (c) A mild fever slows the multiplication of some microbes and speeds up the body's defensive reactions. (d) Mucus and cilia are physical (mechanical) barriers - mucus traps microbes and the beating cilia sweep them out of the airway.
questions.explanation: Tests interferons, fever and physical barriers in a viral infection.

questions.question: Every spring a person begins to sneeze, with a running nose, watery eyes and itching, whenever there is pollen in the air. A doctor explains that the immune system is over-reacting to the pollen and prescribes an antihistamine. (a) What name is given to this over-reaction? (b) What is the pollen called here? (c) Which antibody and which chemical are responsible for the symptoms? (d) What is a sudden, severe, whole-body form of such a reaction called?
questions.answer: (a) The over-reaction is called an allergy (hypersensitivity). (b) The pollen is called an allergen. (c) The antibody responsible is IgE, which attaches to mast cells; on exposure to the allergen these cells release histamine, which causes the sneezing, running nose, watery eyes and itching. (d) A sudden, severe, whole-body allergic reaction is called anaphylaxis.
questions.explanation: Applies allergy concepts: allergen, IgE, histamine and anaphylaxis.
